content.text2: Studio-grade film reviews, without booking a theatre
content.text3: Movie Colab is Viga's production management platform, where film and animation teams track shots and review each other's work on web and mobile. A monitor can make a movie shot look better than it actually is, hiding grain and evening out contrast. Studios book or build theatres to review in-production shots properly, and everyone below that budget reviews on a laptop. At Viga we're trying to democratize filmmaking for teams of any size, so we brought that review room into a Meta Quest headset, with photorealistic theatres, playback synced for everyone so a team in different cities sees the same frame, and annotations the whole room can see. Production heads review in VR, while the artists they review stay on web and mobile, so we had to design for both. I've owned design on it since we started in September '25, designing in Figma for a graphics engineer building in Unity.
Before getting to any features, I had to figure out how to design for a headset in Figma at all, which came with its own questions:
points: How far a panel should sit from the user, and how big it needs to be at that distance. From testing, 1m worked best, with text at 16px and 14px from Meta's standards
When a screen should attach to an object, and when it should float in the theatre. Frequent controls attach to the hand, larger panels float
How to orient panels so users aren't turning their heads for a basic task. Panels are locked on the x and y axes but not z, which keeps motion sickness down
How to show a 3D experience on a flat frame, so the graphics engineer could build what I meant. Concept frames placed each panel inside the theatre as it would appear in the headset
Which patterns from other VR apps work once you're actually in a headset, which the research below covers

content.text3: We audited existing VR products, most of which aren't direct competitors, and picked up what each one did well. Bigscreen VR for immersion, Skybox VR for simplicity, and Screening Room for how it handles review and commenting inside the headset. From there I set up a system for designing 2D panels and interactions in Figma, with concept frames that showed how they'd look in VR. The first two iterations were non-standard and not accessible for all users, so for the third we switched to Meta's UI system and VR standards as the base. That also gave us their accessibility and interaction guidelines, which helped a lot with keeping things comfortable and not nauseating.

content.caption: Initial conceptualisation of the headset experience in Figma
An early iteration, before we rebuilt the panels on Meta's UI system and standards for VR

content.text2: Keep the theatre, float the rest
content.text3: We had to carry over workflows from Movie Colab Projects on web to stay consistent, and the easy route was to just project the web app onto the theatre screen. But that breaks immersion, the film and the UI end up fighting for the same screen, and everyone in the room is stuck looking at one interface. So I went mixed. The theatre and its screen stay as they are, and panels pop up in the space around you, so each person gets their own interface without touching what's on the big screen. Keeping the environment separate also means theatres can be swapped in as modules. We have standard, IMAX, 3D and 360 theatres so far, and we built a model of the Las Vegas Sphere for Sphere clients, so studios can review there without actually booking the Sphere.

content.caption: Panels and interfaces across the app

content.text3: Play, pause, moving between frames and opening panels get used constantly, so they had to be quick to reach. A popup menu didn't make sense, it's distracting and constantly in your face, so I attached the menu to the left controller and you point at it with the right, kind of like reaching over to the controls on a stereo. Basically Fitts's Law in 3D, the stuff you use most stays closest to your hand. Options are ordered by how often they're used, and the menu is modular so we can add more options and layers later. Common actions like switching a shot or sequence from the review panel also update instantly.

content.caption: Three iterations of the hand menu, from rough concept to the final layout

content.text3: The goal was to make the whole app usable with just two buttons, menu and trigger. Everything else, like play and pause, is a quick keybind that's also in the menu. Two buttons is easy to sell to a first time user, there isn't much to remember. For when people still got stuck, we added infotips, a help section with a video demo for each interaction, and a controls panel on the login page.

Reviewers draw on a shot to show artists what to change, more like doodling on the frame than writing a note. They do it a lot, so there are two ways to start one. The first is drawing straight on the theatre screen while paused, so everyone in the theatre sees it, and that opens the annotation panel where you can change brush color, add a message and submit. The second starts from the panel, where you take a frameshot and annotate it right in front of you.

content.caption: Reviewing and commenting on a shot version in the headset

content.text3: Sessions are recorded and transcribed by our diarisation engine, and they show up on web and mobile rather than in VR, since that's where the artists actually work. The session viewer shows the audio and transcription next to the reviewed version, synced to both the session and annotation timestamps, so artists can hear what was said while seeing what was drawn. We recently added a comment viewer too, which pulls comments from whichever shot version is on screen, so the assigned artist can start on feedback while the session is still going.

content.caption: Session viewer on web, with transcription synced to annotations

content.text3: Meta's standards and the apps we audited helped a lot, but some of what we needed just wasn't documented anywhere. The biggest one is getting the context of a review done in 3D over to an artist who sees it in 2D. A flat frame with a note loses most of the spatial and audio context, and that context could also be used for automation, like turning a review straight into tasks for artists once it's done. Most VR guidance is also written for games and casual use, not for people doing the same expert task for hours, which is something I want to keep working on.

An executive from Prologue, an Emmy Award winning VFX studio, told us it's the best user experience in this segment on the market right now, and artists have been just as positive. Next up is immersion, getting interactions closer to how polished visionOS feels, and better hands-only input, which is pretty minimal in the app right now.
